HORTSCIENCE 61(7):1569–1574. 2026. https://doi.org/10.21273/HORTSCI19150-25 Long-term Use of Athletic Field Paint Affects Soil Physical Properties

Audrey Young, Erick Begitschke, Alberto Novello, Chih Julie Wang, Matthew Thibodeaux, Nandita Gaur, and Gerald Henry Department of Crop and Soil Sciences, University of Georgia, 3111 Miller Plant Science Building, Athens, GA 30602, USA

Keywords. bulk density, ﬁeld capacity, ﬁeld paint, saturated hydraulic conductivity, sports ﬁelds, turfgrass, volumetric water content, wilting point

Abstract. Applying athletic ﬁeld paint is a routine practice that turfgrass managers perform to provide boundary lines and aesthetics for various sporting events. However, paint components, such as pigments, resins, solvents, and additives, accumulate within the soil with each application and may progressively disrupt turfgrass and soil function. Therefore, the objective of our research was to determine the potential effects of painting on fundamental physical soil health characteristics: bulk density, ﬁeld capacity, saturated hydraulic conductivity, and wilting point. Laboratory testing was conducted with soil samples obtained from painted and nonpainted areas of four high school football ﬁelds built with US Golf Association speciﬁcations in the Metro Atlanta area in Georgia. While signiﬁcant differences varied, trends of certain soil parameter medians were observed between ﬁelds. Bulk density was higher in painted samples compared with nonpainted samples in three of the four ﬁelds. Although not always signiﬁcant, ﬁeld capacity was higher for nonpainted areas in three of the four ﬁelds. However, for wilting point and saturated hydraulic conductivity, two ﬁelds had higher values for painted areas, while the other two ﬁelds had higher values for nonpainted areas. Increases in bulk density may occur in response to painting applications, further contributing to the variability of ﬁeld soil parameters and potentially heightening athlete injuries and reducing playability. Therefore, changes in cultural practices aimed at alleviating soil compaction and surface hardness like aeriﬁcation may be necessary in painted areas of the ﬁeld.

Introduction

Turfgrass managers apply athletic paints to ﬁeld surfaces to create boundary lines and logos that provide direction and aesthetics for a range of sporting events (Puhalla et al. 2010). Most of these paints are water-based acrylic latex containing a variety of pigments, resins, solvents, and additives, so application is required weekly during ﬁeld play (Hartmann et al. 2019; Reynolds et al. 2012). Although responsible for different chemical functions, each of these paint constituents has the potential to disrupt turfgrass and soil function. Furthermore, it has been suggested that paints should be considered a source of microplastics since they contain polymer binders

(Cunningham et al. 2020; Hartmann et al. 2019; Xu et al. 2022). The accumulation of paint over time has been previously associated with disruption of light in the visible spectrum reaching the leaf surface and, therefore, a decrease in the photosynthetic activity of the turfgrass canopy (Reynolds et al. 2012). In fact, Segars and Moss (2014) observed a reduction in photosynthesis when turfgrass foliage was covered in darker paint colors, while canopy temperatures increased in response to the colors black and green. Decreases in photosynthetic activity often translate to reductions in turfgrass quality through canopy thinning (McBee 1969). Reductions in leaf water-soluble carbohydrate content and leaf transpiration in response to paint presence further demonstrate potential long-term impacts on turfgrass health (Reynolds et al. 2016; Segars et al. 2024). Hollow-core aeriﬁcation practices conducted on sand-based soil proﬁles often reveal paint migration from surface applications to depths approaching 15 cm. This has been conﬁrmed through several social media posts depicting pictures of collegiate ﬁelds following aeriﬁcation or soil samples obtained by university turfgrass managers (personal observation). Monetary costs, labor, and disruption in play often limit the frequency of athletic ﬁeld renovation; therefore, paint penetration can be exacerbated over time. Athletic ﬁeld paints often contain claybased pigments and latex binders. It is well established that increasing clay content generally

decreases effective pore diameter by blocking larger pores, thereby increasing soil water retention and ﬁeld capacity while reducing saturated hydraulic conductivity (Arya and Paris 1981; Awedat et al. 2021; Rawls and Brakensiek 1989; Saxton and Rawls 2006). Similarly, latex and acrylic binders can alter soil physical properties by coating soil particles, bridging aggregates, and modifying pore-size distribution (Park et al. 2021), which in turn affects hydraulic conductivity, inﬁltration, aggregate stability, and water retention behavior (Andry et al. 2009). In engineered sand and turfgrass root zones, polymer amendments have also been shown to increase moisture retention by altering pore connectivity and capillary ﬂow pathways (Alvarez et al. 2016). Thus, it is theorized that athletic ﬁeld paint can modify soil physical properties of sports ﬁelds and consequently affect functionality. Soil characteristics such as bulk density, ﬁeld capacity, saturated hydraulic conductivity, and wilting point are key physical parameters for the quantiﬁcation of soil functionality within a turfgrass system. Field capacity, deﬁned as the amount of water held by soil following the cessation of spontaneous downward movement of water, helps determine effective plant-available water (Veihmeyer and Hendrickson 1949). Decreases in ﬁeld capacity could initiate acute drought stress, reduce nutrient uptake, and limit root proliferation (Fang et al. 2017; Mbagwu and Osuigwe 1985). Saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat) is a measure of how readily water can pass through saturated soil and can be used to determine athletic ﬁeld drainage (Usowicz and Lipiec 2021). Decreases in saturated hydraulic conductivity might result in oxygen deﬁciency, reduced nutrient availability, and root inhibition (Arvidsson 1999; Dexter et al. 2004). Application variability of painting practices in combination with potential changes to soil physical properties and function may further complicate turfgrass management and athletic ﬁeld performance. Irrigation inputs may result in uneven ﬁeld saturation while compromised root growth can decrease playability and subsequently increase the probability of athlete injuries. The identiﬁcation of speciﬁc soil characteristics affected by the presence of athletic ﬁeld paint could modify current management practices to account for within-ﬁeld variability. Therefore, the objective of our research was to determine whether the presence of athletic ﬁeld paint within the soil proﬁle affects soil physical properties and functionality.

Materials and Methods

Field descriptions. Research was conducted in the summer of 2024 at four natural grass sports ﬁelds located throughout the Metro Atlanta area in Georgia. 84.2165W). Fields measured 48.8 m  109.7 m and were primarily used for varsity level sports including American football, soccer, and lacrosse. No renovation was conducted within the past 5 years, and all ﬁelds were surfaced with hybrid bermudagrass [Cynodon dactylon (L.) Pers.  Cynodon transvaalensis Burtt-Davy]. The hybrid bermudagrass cultivars at each location were as follows: ‘Tifway’ at Pace Academy, the Westminster Schools, and Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School and ‘TifTuf’ at Wesleyan School. Perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne L.) was overseeded yearly in the fall on each ﬁeld at a rate of 391 to 586 kg·ha1. Each ﬁeld was constructed to US Golf Association (USGA) speciﬁcations with a 31- to 41-cm depth sand root zone (9:1 sand to peat mixture) placed above a 10-cm gravel layer with a drainage system installed below for the removal of excess water. Management practices for all locations included weekly irrigation at 2.5 cm/week and regular painting of ﬁeld boundary lines and school logos. A composite sample of 16 soil cores (four 2.5-cm diameter soil cores to a depth of 12.7 cm) were obtained across each ﬁeld, air-dried for 48 h, sieved through a 2-mm mesh screen, and sent to the University of Georgia Agricultural and Environmental Services Laboratories in Athens, GA, for analysis (Table 1). Field ages (since last renovation) and number of painting applications per year are presented in Table 2. Field managers used Graco LineLazer 3400 (Graco Inc., Minneapolis, MN, USA) or Titan PowrLiner 3500 (Wager Spraytech Corp., Plymouth, MN, USA) gas-powered, airless paint applicators to apply AquaSTRIPE #2B extra bright (US Specialty Coatings, Alpharetta, GA, USA) or World Class Athletic white ﬁeld paint (World Class Athletic Surfaces, Inc., Forest Hill, MD, USA) at 10,342 to 13,790 kPa. Sample collection. Volumetric water content (%VWC) maps were created to guide sampling areas within each ﬁeld to account for any underlying conditions related to soil moisture. A FieldScout TDR 300 soil moisture meter (Spectrum Technologies, Inc., Aurora, IL, USA) was used to record %VWC measurements on a 9-m  9-m grid. Three readings were taken in close proximity to each other at each grid point to ensure that no outliers resulted from soil macropores. Readings were georeferenced with a global positioning system (GPS) unit (Trimble Inc., Westminster, CO, USA). Soil moisture (%VWC) data were analyzed with ArcGIS Pro version 3.2.0 (ESRI, Redlands, CA, USA). Soil moisture data based

on the observed range of values in our four ﬁelds were interpolated using the inverse distance weighting method to create continuous raster maps. The soil moisture range in which samples were collected at each location were as follows: 20% to 30%VWC at Pace Academy and Wesleyan School, 40% to 45%VWC at the Westminster Schools, and 12% to 25%VWC at Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School. The soil samples for the physical property analysis were collected from locations with similar %VWC to help reduce sample variability. Eight nonpainted and eight painted samples were collected with sampling rings (6-cm height and 5.4-cm diameter; SoilMoisture Equipment Corporation, Santa Barbara, CA, USA). The rings were hammered into the ground using a rubber mallet and a wooden block for stability until the top of the ring was ﬂush with the soil surface. The rings were then dug out of the ground, and any remaining soil on the bottom of the ring was leveled with a soil knife before being sealed with plastic wrap to maintain the integrity of the ﬁeld weight before and during transport. The samples were refrigerated at 4 C until laboratory experiments were initiated. Laboratory testing. The soil tests were collected in the order they are mentioned below. To expel all air from the soil sample and ensure complete saturation, each sample was saturated from the bottom up by placing the soil samples in a water bath without covering the top of the sample (Klute 1986). Saturated hydraulic conductivity. Ksat was then calculated using the automated, Chameleon single-station system and the associated monitor transducer software (SoilMoisture Equipment Corporation) using the constant head method (Reynolds and Elrick 2002). To calibrate the system, an empty sample ring was set up in a Tempe cell system that was attached to a water reservoir. A zero head height was established by lowering the air tube into the water reservoir

until the Tempe cell stopped dripping and the air tube stopped bubbling. The zero head height was used as a reference when setting the desired constant head height of 8.5 cm. The samples were allowed to fully saturate and stabilize by turning on the water reservoir valve until the system started dripping at a constant rate and the air tube was bubbling. After saturation, the monitor transducer was connected to the Chameleon software, and data points were collected in 10 equal increments and allowed to run for 10 min according to the operating instructions (SoilMoisture Equipment Corporation 2016). After the reading period was complete, the ﬁrst and last collected data points were used to calculate an average Ksat value in cm·min1. Field capacity. Following sample saturation during the Ksat process, each sample ring was set up in another Tempe cell system with a ceramic plate (SoilMoisture Equipment Corporation) to calculate ﬁeld capacity. Any moisture held by the soil at a suction higher than 33 kPa was assumed to represent ﬁeld capacity according to standard National Resource Conservation Survey recommendations. The Tempe cells were attached to air tubes that supplied pressure at a constant rate of 33 kPa. Any detectable pressure leaks in the system were sealed with paraﬁlm (American Can Co., Greenwich, CT, USA). The samples were removed from the system after 48 h of pressure or until water no longer dripped from the system. Wilting point. The WP4C Dewpoint PotentiaMeter (METER Group, Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) was used to gather wilting point values, i.e. moisture held within the soil at a suction higher than 1500 kPa. This sensor measured relative humidity that was later converted to soil matric potential using the Kelvin equation at two different known soil wetness conditions. Care was taken to ensure that the matric potentials at both conditions were lower than 100 kPa. Further, leveraging the linear relationship between the logarithm of water content and the logarithm of water potential when drier than 100 kPa, the soil water content at a matric potential of 1500 kPa was calculated from the measured values. To perform this test, air-dried soil was placed into a stainless-steel sample cup until the bottom of the cup was covered and the cup was half full. Any soil particles on the rim of the cup were cleaned off with a Kimwipe (Kimberly-Clark Professionals, Irving, TX, USA). Following the operating instructions of the device, the sample cup was placed in the machine and allowed to warm until the difference between the temperature of the sample and the temperature of the chamber block (Ts  Tb) was between 0.50 and 0. Once at a desirable temperature, the sample reading was initiated and run on precise mode. After the ﬁrst run, 1 to 2.5 ml of deionized water was added to the sample, and the process was repeated. Matric potential values (in megapascals) from dry and wet readings were recorded and used with their corresponding water contents to calculate the water content at wilting point. Data analysis. All data analyses were conducted in R version 4.3.1 (RStudio, Inc., Boston, MA, USA). The data points were insufﬁcient to conduct any parametric tests; therefore, nonparametric tests were used for a majority of the data analysis. As such, the Kruskal–Wallis test was used to test for within-school variability using the kruskal.test function to determine signiﬁ- cant differences between the medians of three or more independent groups (Kruskal and Wallis 1952). An H-statistic, given to determine variance in ranks, closely follows the v2

distribution (McKight and Najab 2010). Two soil samples had a measured ﬁeld capacity

value of zero resulting from air leaks in the Tempe cell apparatus and hence were deleted from the data set, but no values were removed from any other soil physical properties that were tested.

Results and Discussion

Bulk density. Bulk density of painted samples was signiﬁcantly different from nonpainted samples at Pace Academy, the Westminster Schools, and Wesleyan School (Table 3). In terms of effect sizes, the median bulk density in painted samples was higher than nonpainted samples across all schools except Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School. This aligns with our theorized understanding that acrylic-latex–based paints introduce synthetic polymers and heavy pigments, which may decrease soil porosity by displacing gas-ﬁlled pores with denser solid materials (Jannesarahmadi et al. 2023; Xu et al. 2022). Unlike our results, Ogle (2020) observed no differences in bulk density when investigating the inﬂuence of nozzle size and pressure (3447 to 10,342 kPa) of acrylic-latex– based paint applications on the soil properties of two 4-year-old hybrid bermudagrass football ﬁelds established on USGA sand-based root zones. However, measurements in their research were only obtained following a total of eight paint applications. While these results appear contradictory, they both follow our theorized understanding. Changes in bulk density depend on the soil’s textural and organic matter composition, as these determine the original pore size distribution altered by the addition of clay and polymer binders. It will also depend on the amount of paint added to the soil, which in turn depends on the number and type of paint applications. Therefore, a threshold may need to be met in terms of the total paint application amount necessary to cause differences in bulk density between painted and nonpainted samples, and this threshold may vary with the original composition of the ﬁeld. In our research, clay contents were similar in all schools except for Wesleyan School, which had the lowest clay content (1.08%) compared with the other schools (2.08%). Organic matter content in soils at Pace Academy and the Westminster Schools was similar (2.26% to 2.58%), and it was highest (3.62%) at Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School and lowest at Wesleyan School (0.56%). Therefore, it can be theorized that Wesleyan School had bigger pores compared with the other schools, which aligns with the fact that it was most recently renovated (5 years ago). An additional mechanistic explanation for the lack of differences in bulk density at Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School is that since organic matter is much lighter and more porous than sand particles, a greater accumulation of organic matter increases soil volume more than it increases mass (Soane 1990). Collectively, these conditions explain why we found statistically higher differences in painted surfaces in all schools except for Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School. While no other studies assessed comparisons between painted and nonpainted surfaces,

the increases in bulk density observed in our research were consistent with the addition of other soil non–water-soluble pollutants. For example, Abosede (2013) reported a 7.1% increase in bulk density of loamy sand soil when contaminated with crude oil compared with nonpolluted soil. Therefore, the addition of athletic ﬁeld paint, whether contributing resins or clays to the soil proﬁle, like pollutants, may modify soil structure and thereby lead to an increase in bulk density. However, the existence of both microplastic and soil characteristic heterogeneity may further complicate the impact assessment of plastic-induced changes that occur to soil properties beyond our experimental conditions. Field capacity. Field capacity in sandy systems increases with clay and organic matter content (Rawls et al. 2003). Consequently, in line with expectations, ﬁeld capacity values for nonpainted samples at Pace Academy (0.31 m3·m3) and the Westminster Schools (0.31 m3·m3) were higher than Wesleyan School (0.26 m3·m3). Featuring the highest organic matter and clay content, Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School (0.16 m3·m3) again deviated from traditional expectations, even among nonpainted samples. At this point, it is important to note that the ﬁeld at Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School was not as regularly maintained as the other ﬁelds in the study. Variability in the maintenance of turfgrass ﬁelds leading to variability in soil compaction was previously documented by Craft et al. (2017) and Brown et al. (2016). Since paints also add clay and latex binders to the soil system, we theorized that pore size distribution would become further constricted, resulting in an increase in ﬁeld capacity for soils receiving paint applications. However, this was only observed for the Westminster Schools. While signiﬁcant differences were only observed between painted and nonpainted samples at the Westminster Schools and Wesleyan School, the results were opposite, with nonpainted samples exhibiting greater ﬁeld capacity at Wesleyan School (Table 3); however, the effect size across all four schools indicated a general decrease in ﬁeld capacity with the addition of paint. We hypothesize that this contradictory impact may result from the chemical nature of paint binders (resins and polymers). While they may adhere to sand particles, subsequently reducing interconnected voids within the soil proﬁle, they also increase hydrophobicity via paint additives like alkyl amines (Hartmann et al. 2019; Jannesarahmadi et al. 2023; Kim et al. 2024), thus not allowing the pores to effectively retain water. Field capacity measurements are inversely related to the bulk density of soils (Archer and Smith 1972). Some of our results comply with this classic relationship between ﬁeld capacity and bulk density. Consistent with this observation, May (2019) observed a shift to larger sand particle sizes in response to more frequent applications of acrylic-latex–based paint to Kentucky bluegrass (Poa pratensis L.) and perennial ryegrass mixtures grown on sand-based root zones. Wang et al. (2020) observed a reduction in soil water holding capacity of three soil textures (sandy, sandy loam, and loam) in response to the presence of residual plastic ﬁlm, while Qi et al. (2020) noted inconsistent ﬁeld capacity responses of sandy soils to the presence of low-density polyethylene mulch. Additionally, paint in our research was observed evenly distributed throughout excavated soil samples to depths approaching 15 cm, which may have reduced the impervious surface response (altered ﬁeld capacity and water inﬁltration) typically observed in some native soils containing a more concentrated layer of paint near the soil surface (Hillel 2013). Saturated hydraulic conductivity. Again, consistent with the expected relationship between sand, organic matter, and clay content, Wesleyan School had the highest saturated hydraulic conductivity. Like ﬁeld capacity, the saturated hydraulic conductivity of Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School also did not conform to traditional expectations, indicating that irregular maintenance practices may negatively affect the soil physical properties of the ﬁeld. Saturated hydraulic conductivity was only signiﬁcantly different at the Westminster Schools and Pace Academy with nonpainted samples resulting in higher Ksat values than painted samples at the Westminster Schools, but the opposite was observed for Pace Academy (Table 3). These results align with the results of ﬁeld capacity and are consistent with our hypothesis of increased hydrophobicity causing a decrease in ﬁeld capacity and a corresponding increase in hydraulic conductivity. Hydrophobicity often has contradictory effects on hydraulic conductivity, but it has been shown that when coatings smooth sand grain particles, hydrophobicity can signiﬁcantly increase hydraulic conductivity (Xing et al. 2026). This indicates that two contradictory mechanisms are at play when considering ﬁeld capacity and saturated hydraulic conductivity. While the addition of clay and latex additives tend to reduce conductivity and increase ﬁeld capacity by physically blocking larger pores, the chemical nature of the pigment can negate the effects of decreasing pore size by creating hydrophobicity. Other studies have also reported similar contradictory results. May (2019) observed reduced inﬁltration in response to paint despite the limited number of applications made in their research. One painting per month (2.6 cm 15 min1) resulted in a lower inﬁltration rate than all other treatments. Four paintings per month (2.7 cm 15 min1) resulted in a 0.9% lower inﬁltration rate than both the nonpainted control (2.9 cm 15 min1) and two paintings per month (3.1 cm 15 min1). Similarly, Guo et al. (2022) noted a 96%

reduction in Ksat of sand subjected to polypropylene microplastics, while Qi et al. (2020) reported an increase in Ksat resulting from the addition of low-density polyethylene mulch to a sandy soil. Wilting point. A signiﬁcant difference between painted and nonpainted samples with respect to wilting point was observed at Wesleyan School, where nonpainted samples were higher, and Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School, where the trend was opposite (Table 3). Much like Ksat, there were no clear consistent effect sizes. Similarly, Bakhshaee et al. (2025) reported that microplastic contamination had minimal impact on wilting point, regardless of plastic particle size; however, this may not be true with plants that are less water resistant. Research limitations. The inconsistent trends observed for soil parameters between analyzed ﬁelds may be associated with inherent variability due to management techniques, speciﬁc sports, or construction/renovation. Fields with similar construction (soil proﬁles and drainage) and level of sport were chosen to limit variability. Soil moisture maps were also created to direct the sampling process; however, additional sensor data including surface hardness and penetration resistance may have provided further guidance. During saturated hydraulic conductivity testing in the laboratory, the Chameleon automatic system occasionally skipped readings, which may have affected the computed average Ksat values. Finally, additional samples or more replicates could be collected to perform a more robust parametric statistical analysis.

Conclusions

Although several studies have evaluated the impact of athletic ﬁeld paint on plant physiology, few have investigated the inﬂuence of acrylic-latex–based paint presence on soil physical properties. Paint application to athletic ﬁelds may cause an increase in soil bulk density over time. Since paint is not applied uniformly across ﬁelds, this may increase surface hardness and soil compaction variability, further complicating ﬁeld playability and athlete safety. Straw et al. (2018) reported a potential relationship between ground-derived athlete injuries and surface hardness variability, with most injuries occurring in areas of transition between nonsigniﬁcant and signiﬁcantly low and high surface hardness values. Routine aeriﬁcation applications have been shown to decrease bulk density (Atkinson et al. 2012); therefore, soil cultivation practices may be required more frequently to reduce negative impacts of paint presence within the soil proﬁle. Targeted or site-speciﬁc aeriﬁcation may be employed on more intensively painted ﬁeld locations including school logos, numbers, and endzones. Fraise mowing is a more commonly conducted cultural practice for the removal of signiﬁcant thatch layers or the reduction of annual bluegrass infestations (Aldous et al. 2014; Brosnan et al. 2020; Carroll et al. 2021). This may be appropriate when invasive cultivation strategies cannot be employed; however, this is not a solution for soil compaction, and sequential applications may be necessary.
